review.name: Principles of American Government
review.lo: LO 1.6.A — Explain the constitutional principles of separation of powers and checks and balances.  |  LO 1.6.B — Explain the effects of separation of powers and checks and balances for the U.S. political system.
review.core: The framers assumed officeholders would pursue their own interests, so they built a structure in which ambition in one branch runs into ambition in another. The design produces friction on purpose.
blocks: Government is divided into three branches, each with its own function. Congress makes law, the executive carries it out, the courts interpret it. This is the structure.

Each branch holds powers that restrain the others, so no branch becomes too powerful. This is what happens within the structure. Creating the judiciary is separation of powers; the judiciary striking down a statute is a check.

Madison explains how these provisions control potential abuses by majorities. Ambition must be made to counteract ambition; the interest of the officeholder must be tied to the constitutional rights of the office. He also warns that the legislative branch tends to dominate and must be checked accordingly.

Multiple access points — because authority is spread across institutions, stakeholders defeated in one arena can try another, which gives organized interests more opportunities to shape policy. Accountability for abuse of power — the House impeaches by majority vote, formally charging an official with abuse of power or misconduct; the Senate tries the case and may convict and remove by a two-thirds vote.
traps: Separation of powers versus checks and balances
Structure versus action. If the answer describes one branch acting on another, it is a check.

These get swapped constantly, and they are not close. Separation of powers divides authority among the three branches — legislative, executive, judicial — all at the same level of government. Federalism divides authority between levels — national and state. If the scenario involves Congress and the president, it is separation of powers. If it involves Washington and a state capital, it is federalism.
An official impeached by the House but acquitted by the Senate stays in office. Use the words precisely on free-response questions.
